As of 229 PM Saturday... 

KEY MESSAGE 1... Isaias remnants and resulting rains underway, 
continuing tonight. 

The large-scale circulation and pattern assoc with Isaias remnants 
is resulting in patchy light rain across central NC attm. Meanwhile, 
central NC remains under the influence of a stable wedge airmass, 
thus the reason for the lack of convection so far.  NWP thermodynamic 
fields suggest that the low level wedge will remain in place most of 
tonight, while the H8 front will lift north across central NC early 
this evening with vigorous and warming H8 flow overnight. This 
overrunning setup suggests that the patchy rain we're seeing now may 
become more occasional tonight, with perhaps some elevated 
convection at times which could result in scattered heavier 
downpours and heavier rain rates.  But in terms of surface-based 
convection... that should hold off until the daytime Sunday. So in 
summary, look for ongoing likelihood for rain tonight, with some 
scattered pockets of heavier rain and even a few rumbles of thunder 
possible. It's also worth noting that NE to E sfc wind gusts of 20-
25 mph will remain possible through this evening before relaxing a 
bit overnight.  

KEY MESSAGE 2... Scattered to locally numerous showers/storms late 
Sun morning into the early evening hours will be capable of brief, 
short-tracked tornadoes and strong to severe wind gusts.

A staked low, containing the remnants of post-tropical cyclone 
Isaias, will be positioned over KY/TN by 12z Sun morning. CAD 
erosion should be well underway Sun morning with a west-northwest 
positioning of the surface low relative to central NC and retreating 
surface high over the Canadian maritimes. This configuration should 
support a warm front lifting northward through NC Sun morning and 
into VA by Sun afternoon; although given the close proximity of the 
primary surface low, wouldn't be surprised to see the CAD wedge hold 
over the far NW Piedmont and Foothills of the NC/VA mountains as 
secondary cyclogenesis develops along the warm front from Mt. Airy 
into northern/central VA.

Widespread multi-layered cloud cover may limit destabilization a 
bit, but theta-e advection within the warm sector should be able to 
overcome this limitation as surface dew points surge into the 
low/mid 70s and supports 500-1500 SBCAPE. Convection is expected to 
develop along and ahead of the trailing cold front late Sun morning 
and may continue into early Sun evening (10 AM until 8 PM). A belt 
of 40-60 kt southwesterly mid-lvl winds will overspread the 
Carolinas into VA throughout the daylight hours and support a 
kinematic environment favorable for organized convection given 
adequate thermodynamic parameters. Shear vectors oriented roughly 45 
degrees to the initiating boundary, trailing cold front, would 
support discrete supercellular storm mode given limited storm 
collisions/interactions.

A stout 25-35 kt low-lvl jet at 925mb overtop of the warm sector 
will provide elongation of the low-lvl hodograph and support 100-150 
m2/s2 0-1 km SRH across most locations, which is a bit on the low-
end but could still produce a short-lived tornado anywhere within 
the warm sector. The greater localized tornado threat will likely 
occur where surface winds back from the south to more of a southeast 
direction and results in +200 m2/s2 0-1km SRH. This is most likely 
to materialize along and just south of the warm front and nearest 
the triple point with the secondary surface low (as far west as the 
Triad, across the northern Piedmont into the Triangle and continuing 
into the northern Coastal Plain and more likely northward into VA).

The big caveat will be the intrusion of drier air in the mid/upper 
lvls over the Carolinas. Already limited instability would be 
further truncated by dry air intrusion into updrafts and greatly 
limiting their updraft strength, which may not survive the strong 
shear in place. Deep convection will be more likely further south 
into the moderate instability across the Sandhills, up into the 
Triangle and across the Coastal Plain which may more likely overcome 
the dry air aloft, but is farther removed from the more favorable 
low-lvl kinematics to support anything more than a quick spinup and 
short-track tornado threat.

KEY MESSAGE 3... Unseasonably warm Monday through Wednesday night 
for mid-October.

In between the departing mid/upper level low over the Atlantic, 
which absorbed TC Isaias, and closed low expected to develop/deepen 
over the Central Intermountain West, mid/upper level subtropical 
ridge will bubble northeastward from the ArkLaTex region into the 
Southeast Tues into Thurs. A low-amplitude disturbance, and 
associated area of surface low pressure, racing across the 
International Border with Canada Tues through Wed will also spread 
anomalously warm H850 temperatures in place over the MS and western 
OH Valley's on Mon over the Mid-Atlantic on Tues before shifting 
south over the Carolinas
